payload.set_intro: A researcher recruited 50 first-year college students who all disagreed with a proposed rule that would require every student to attend a 7:00 A.M. exercise class. Using random assignment, she placed 25 students in each of two conditions. Each student recorded an audio message urging classmates to support the rule. Students in the first condition were paid $2 for the recording, and students in the second condition were paid $40. Afterward, an assistant who did not know which payment each student had received asked the student to rate his or her own agreement with the rule from 1 (strongly disagree) to 9 (strongly agree). The table shows the results.

stimulus.description: Agreement with the rule by payment condition

items.stem: Which concept best explains why the students paid $2 reported more agreement with the rule than the students paid $40?

options.text: Cognitive dissonance reduction
options.why: Students paid very little had weak outside justification for arguing against their own view, so they may have shifted their attitude to reduce the tension between their behavior and their belief.

options.text: The central route to persuasion
options.why: The central route changes attitudes through careful evaluation of argument quality, but the payment amount says nothing about argument quality.

options.text: The foot-in-the-door phenomenon
options.why: That phenomenon involves agreeing to a small request first, which raises later compliance with a larger request, and no larger request was made here.

options.text: The fundamental attribution error
options.why: That error is overemphasizing personality and underemphasizing situations when explaining other people's behavior, which is not what the ratings measure.

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is Cognitive dissonance reduction. Students paid very little had weak outside justification for arguing against their own view, so they may have shifted their attitude to reduce the tension between their behavior and their belief.
The central route to persuasion is incorrect: The central route changes attitudes through careful evaluation of argument quality, but the payment amount says nothing about argument quality.
The foot-in-the-door phenomenon is incorrect: That phenomenon involves agreeing to a small request first, which raises later compliance with a larger request, and no larger request was made here.
The fundamental attribution error is incorrect: That error is overemphasizing personality and underemphasizing situations when explaining other people's behavior, which is not what the ratings measure.

payload.set_intro: A 24-year-old graduate student sought help because she could not leave her apartment without checking the stove and the door lock over and over. She knew the checks were unnecessary, but skipping them made her intensely anxious, and the routine made her late to class most mornings. A clinician asked her to record the total minutes she spent checking on a typical day and then worked with her in weekly sessions. The table shows her self-recorded daily checking time at three points.

items.stem: Which disorder best fits the student's symptoms?

options.text: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
options.why: Repeated checking performed to relieve intense anxiety, even though the person recognizes it as unnecessary, is characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder.

options.text: Panic disorder
options.why: That disorder involves sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms, not a daily routine of checking.

options.text: Major depressive disorder
options.why: That disorder centers on persistent low mood or loss of interest, which the description does not mention.

options.text: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.why: That disorder involves persistent, hard-to-control worry about many topics rather than a repeated ritual performed to relieve anxiety.

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is Obsessive-compulsive disorder. Repeated checking performed to relieve intense anxiety, even though the person recognizes it as unnecessary, is characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
Panic disorder is incorrect: That disorder involves sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms, not a daily routine of checking.
Major depressive disorder is incorrect: That disorder centers on persistent low mood or loss of interest, which the description does not mention.
Generalized anxiety disorder is incorrect: That disorder involves persistent, hard-to-control worry about many topics rather than a repeated ritual performed to relieve anxiety.
